analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal, state-administered national health plan with capped out-of-pocket costs and a federal long-term care program.
analysis.headline: This universal health care bill never received a vote: it sat in two House committees from March 1990 until the Congress ended, and the record points to a different bill for further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made every U.S. citizen and lawful resident eligible to enroll in a state-run health plan covering hospital care, doctor visits, preventive services, mental health and substance abuse treatment, hospice, prescription-adjacent services, and long-term care. States and the federal government would share financing, out-of-pocket costs would be capped, and no cost-sharing at all would be allowed for families below twice the poverty line. Private insurers would be barred from selling coverage that duplicates the basic package, and Medicaid would be replaced in states that set up approved programs. It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured Americans would gain guaranteed enrollment in a health plan covering a broad basic package, with premiums community-rated so sick people could not be charged more, deductibles capped at $200-$500, and no premiums or cost-sharing at all for families under 200% of the poverty line. Elderly and disabled people who need help with daily living would gain a new federal home- and community-based care program, six months of nursing home coverage, and respite care for family caregivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured Americans of all ages

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be eligible to enroll in a state Comprehensive Health Care program, with default enrollment at the point of care for anyone who had not signed up.

Basic coverage would include hospital care, physician and professional services, diagnostic tests, prenatal and well-baby care, mental health services, drug and alcohol treatment, hospice, and long-term care, with states and plans free to add more.

Families with income below 200% of the poverty line could not be charged any premium or cost-sharing; for everyone else, deductibles would be capped at $200 per individual or $500 per family, coinsurance at 20%, and total annual premiums plus cost-sharing at $1,000 per individual or $2,500 per family.
Plan premiums would have to be community-rated and could not reflect the health status of individuals or groups, so people with pre-existing conditions could not be priced out.

A new Lifecare Long-Term Care Protection program would cover home and community-based care, the first six months of nursing home care, and respite care for caregivers, with a consumer bill of rights and quality-assurance requirements for providers.

In states with an approved program, Medicaid would no longer apply, replaced by the broader state plan, and providers would have to accept the program's payment as payment in full, ending balance billing of patients.

analysis.who_pays: State budgets would bear most new financing through general revenues, earmarked or sales taxes, and employer and employee premiums, backed by per-capita federal contributions and start-up grants of $10 million per state. Doctors and hospitals would face payment schedules set in line with state health budgets, mandatory acceptance of program rates, and, for hospitals, prospective biennial budgets and plans to reduce excess beds. Private insurers would lose the market for coverage duplicating the basic package.
analysis.who_pays_short: State budgets, employers, and premium-paying households

drawbacks.text: The bill specifies no dedicated federal tax to pay for universal coverage; financing would rest on state revenues, premiums, and cost-sharing plus federal per-capita contributions tied to past spending, so the true cost to taxpayers and how it would be raised were left largely undefined.

Providers would have to accept program payment as payment in full, hospitals would operate under biennial prospective budgets and state plans to cut excess beds, and physicians would be paid from negotiated fee schedules — a genuine cost in reduced revenue that hospitals and physician groups would have fought.

Basic benefits mirror Medicare's scope, so services Medicare does not cover — routine dental care, eyeglasses, routine physicals beyond preventive services — would be excluded, and federal funding could not be used for anything beyond the basic package.

The program would not start until the third year after enactment, and only if at least half the states had passed implementing legislation, giving states and opponents years of delay before any coverage began.
Mental health coverage would be capped at 45 inpatient days and 20 outpatient visits per year, and states could further limit substance abuse treatment benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — universal coverage with hard caps on what families pay, and protection from health-status rating — would be a large gain for ordinary people, comparable to the reforms other countries adopted decades ago. But the bill was a skeleton: it left financing to states without a revenue mechanism, tied the benefit package closely to Medicare's existing exclusions, delayed benefits for years behind a half-the-states trigger, and would have forced a wrenching transition for hospitals, doctors, and insurers. It was an ambitious, expensive, and politically heavy lift that its 12 supporters never had the votes to move.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees the day it was introduced, then to their health subcommittees, where nothing happened; on November 5, 1990 the record pointed to a different bill for further action, and the 101st Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Rose Oakar introduced the Comprehensive Health Care for All Americans Act, honoring the late Senator Claude Pepper, on March 13, 1990, with four original cosponsors.
The same day it was referred jointly to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees.
Within a week it had been sent to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, the standard path for health bills.
Neither subcommittee took action; the bill accumulated 11 Democratic cosponsors over the session but was never marked up, reported, or debated.
On November 5, 1990 the action record states 'For Further Action See H.R.5835', and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept their market for basic health coverage and employers faced no new financing obligations. The uninsured, underinsured, and families needing long-term care gained nothing, and the problem the bill named went unaddressed for another Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat and no Republican signed on; no votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill bars private insurance from covering anything in the basic package and makes federal employee plans use approved public-program plans, eliminating the core individual and employer market for basic coverage. Insurers' existing revenue from selling basic protection is what the bill replaces, so their interest ran against it.

Hospitals would gain a universal payer for patients now uninsured, but would face biennial prospective budgets negotiated with the state, mandatory acceptance of program rates, and state plans to reduce excess hospital beds with refinancing of hospital debt.

Doctors would gain universally insured patients but be paid from state fee schedules built on a national relative value scale, with mandatory assignment — accepting the payment as payment in full — and no balance billing of patients.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and home care agencies
industries.note: The long-term care division creates a new public entitlement for home- and community-based care and nursing home coverage, with payments flowing only to state-certified agencies and facilities, making them the permanent channel for a new public benefit while imposing certification, staffing, and quality rules on them.

The bill exempts qualified HMOs from state limits on the number of competing plans and directs the national board to encourage organized delivery systems, while universal enrollment would deliver them a large new paying population.
